questions.question: What are the ACID properties of a database transaction?
questions.title: ACID Properties of Database Transactions
questions.direct_answer: ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability — the four properties that guarantee database transactions are processed reliably.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand what each property means and can give a concrete example — not just recite the acronym.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Memorising the definitions without understanding why each matters. Interviewers test with scenario questions: 'what breaks if you remove atomicity?'
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect each property to a real scenario — a bank transfer is the classic example because it illustrates all four clearly.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
I explain ACID using a bank transfer: deducting $100 from Account A and adding $100 to Account B.

Atomicity: the transaction is all-or-nothing. Either both the deduction and the addition happen, or neither does. If the server crashes after the deduction but before the addition, the entire transaction is rolled back. You can't have money disappear from Account A without appearing in Account B.

Consistency: the transaction moves the database from one valid state to another. Business rules are enforced. If a rule says an account balance can't go negative, a transaction that would violate it is rejected — the database remains consistent.

Isolation: concurrent transactions don't interfere with each other. If two transactions are running simultaneously, each sees a consistent view of the data as if the other isn't happening. Without isolation, you could have dirty reads — reading data that another transaction hasn't committed yet.

Durability: once a transaction is committed, it stays committed. Even if the server crashes immediately after commit, the data survives — typically because the commit was written to disk before returning success. You won't 'lose' a committed transaction on a power failure.

In Java with Spring: the @Transactional annotation wraps a method in a transaction and handles rollback on exception, giving you ACID guarantees without writing BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK manually.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Atomicity: all or nothing — partial transactions are rolled back
Consistency: transaction moves DB from one valid state to another, enforces rules
Isolation: concurrent transactions don't see each other's uncommitted changes
Durability: committed data survives crashes — written to persistent storage
Spring @Transactional provides ACID guarantees automatically

followup_questions: What is the difference between a commit and a rollback?
What happens if an exception is thrown inside a @Transactional method?

seo.metaTitle: ACID Properties of Database Transactions | Interview Answer
seo.metaDescription: Learn the ACID properties — Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — with concrete examples and how they apply in Spring Boot.

speakable_v2.standard_example: normalized MySQL schema for a blog app with users, posts, and comments
speakable_v2.hook: ACID is four letters, but each one prevents a different category of data disaster.

beats.text: ACID stands for Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules stay intact), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't interfere), and Durability (committed data survives crashes). Together they guarantee reliable database transactions.
Without ACID, a blog comment insertion that also updates the post's comment_count could succeed halfway — comment saved, count not updated — leaving your data inconsistent with no error thrown.

items: Atomicity: both the comment insert and the count increment commit together or both roll back
Consistency: the count can't go negative — constraints enforce valid state
Isolation: two simultaneous post publishes don't see each other's draft state
Durability: once the transaction commits, a power cut won't undo it

beats.text: In Spring Boot: @Transactional on your service method handles all four. It starts a transaction, runs your repository calls, and commits on success or rolls back on RuntimeException. For our blog's createPost() method that inserts a post AND updates the user's post_count, @Transactional ensures either both happen or neither does. candidates miss: @Transactional doesn't roll back on checked exceptions by default — only on RuntimeException. Add rollbackFor = Exception.class if you need checked exception rollback.

items: Expecting checked exceptions to trigger rollback without rollbackFor — they don't by default
Calling a @Transactional method from within the same class — Spring's proxy is bypassed and transactions won't work

speakable_v2.cap: ACID is what @Transactional delivers — understand all four letters to debug transaction problems confidently.

questions.question: How does Spring's @Transactional annotation work?
questions.title: How @Transactional Works in Spring
questions.direct_answer: @Transactional wraps a method in a database transaction — starting a transaction before the method runs and committing on success or rolling back on unchecked exception.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Spring knowledge — @Transactional is used in almost every Spring Data application.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking @Transactional works when called from within the same class — Spring's AOP proxy doesn't intercept self-invocation.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the self-invocation caveat and explain that @Transactional on private methods also doesn't work — only public methods on Spring beans are proxied.

sections.title: How to Answer
Key Points
content: Spring uses AOP proxy to begin/commit/rollback transactions around @Transactional methods
Default: commit on success, rollback on RuntimeException (unchecked)
Checked exceptions don't rollback by default — use rollbackFor = Exception.class if needed
Self-invocation doesn't work — calling a @Transactional method from within the same class
Only works on public methods of Spring-managed beans

followup_questions: What is transaction propagation in Spring?
Why doesn't @Transactional work on private methods?

seo.metaTitle: How @Transactional Works in Spring | Interview Answer
seo.metaDescription: How Spring's @Transactional annotation works — commit, rollback, self-invocation caveat, and where to place it in a Spring Boot application.

speakable_v2.standard_example: normalized MySQL schema for a blog app with users, posts, and comments
speakable_v2.hook: @Transactional looks simple but has two non-obvious failure modes that trip up almost every Spring newcomer.

beats.text: @Transactional is a Spring annotation that wraps a method in a database transaction using AOP. Spring intercepts the call via a proxy, begins a transaction before the method runs, and commits on success or rolls back on RuntimeException.

Without @Transactional, each repository save() call in your service runs in its own transaction. If the second save() throws an exception, the first one is already committed — your data is now inconsistent.

items: Commits: method returns normally — all DB changes are saved
Rolls back: method throws a RuntimeException — all changes undone
No rollback: method throws a checked Exception — changes ARE committed by default

beats.text: In our blog's publishPost() service method: insert post, increment user.post_count. @Transactional ensures both happen atomically. If incrementing throws an unchecked exception, both operations roll back. In Spring Boot: place @Transactional on public service methods, not on repository methods (they're already transactional). non-obvious: self-invocation doesn't work — if publishPost() calls another @Transactional method in the same class, Spring's proxy isn't involved and a new transaction won't start. You'd need to inject the service into itself or restructure the code.

items: Putting @Transactional on private methods — Spring's proxy can't intercept private methods
Calling @Transactional methods from within the same class (self-invocation) — the proxy is bypassed

speakable_v2.cap: @Transactional is powerful but only works through Spring's proxy — it won't help on private methods or self-calls.
followup_handoff: Why doesn't @Transactional work on private methods?
How do you handle the self-invocation problem with @Transactional?

questions.question: What are the four database transaction isolation levels and what read anomalies do they prevent?
questions.title: Transaction Isolation Levels Explained
questions.direct_answer: The four isolation levels are READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, and SERIALIZABLE — each prevents progressively more read anomalies at the cost of performance.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the trade-off between consistency and performance in concurrent database access.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking SERIALIZABLE is always best — it prevents all anomalies but serialises concurrent transactions, severely hurting throughput.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Know that MySQL's default is REPEATABLE READ and PostgreSQL's default is READ COMMITTED — and be able to say which anomalies each prevents.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
Isolation levels define how much one transaction can see the in-progress work of other concurrent transactions. Higher isolation = more consistency, less concurrency.

READ UNCOMMITTED: a transaction can read data that another transaction has modified but not yet committed. This allows dirty reads — reading data that may be rolled back. Almost never used in practice.

READ COMMITTED: a transaction only reads committed data. No dirty reads. But a row you read twice in the same transaction might return different values if another transaction committed a change between your reads — this is a non-repeatable read. PostgreSQL's default.

REPEATABLE READ: guarantees that if you read a row twice in the same transaction, you get the same value both times. Prevents dirty reads and non-repeatable reads. But you can still get phantom reads — if another transaction inserts new rows, a range query might return different results. MySQL's InnoDB default.

SERIALIZABLE: the strictest level. Transactions appear to run one after another. No dirty reads, no non-repeatable reads, no phantom reads. But it severely reduces concurrency and throughput — transactions may wait or fail if they conflict.

In Spring, set isolation on @Transactional: `@Transactional(isolation = Isolation.READ_COMMITTED)`.

For most OLTP applications, READ COMMITTED is a reasonable default.

sections.title: Key Points
content: READ UNCOMMITTED: allows dirty reads (uncommitted data visible) — rarely used
READ COMMITTED: no dirty reads, allows non-repeatable reads — PostgreSQL default
REPEATABLE READ: no dirty/non-repeatable reads, allows phantom reads — MySQL InnoDB default
SERIALIZABLE: prevents all anomalies, lowest concurrency, highest consistency
Set in Spring: @Transactional(isolation = Isolation.READ_COMMITTED)

seo.metaTitle: Transaction Isolation Levels Explained | Dirty Read, Phantom Read
seo.metaDescription: The four database isolation levels — READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE — and what anomalies each prevents.

speakable_v2.standard_example: normalized MySQL schema for a blog app with users, posts, and comments
speakable_v2.hook: Isolation levels let you trade consistency for concurrency — pick too weak and readers see garbage, pick too strong and throughput tanks.

beats.text: You're balancing data anomaly prevention against concurrent request throughput. Higher isolation prevents more read anomalies but uses more locking, reducing how many transactions can run simultaneously.

items: READ UNCOMMITTED: see uncommitted changes — allows dirty reads, almost never used
READ COMMITTED: see only committed data — prevents dirty reads, PostgreSQL default
REPEATABLE READ: same row read twice gives same value — prevents non-repeatable reads, MySQL InnoDB default
SERIALIZABLE: transactions run as if serial — prevents all anomalies, lowest throughput

beats.text: For our blog, the database defaults (REPEATABLE READ in MySQL, READ COMMITTED in PostgreSQL) are fine. Only move to SERIALIZABLE if a query pattern requires preventing phantom reads — e.g., booking the last available comment slot in a limited series.

items: You see duplicate entries or wrong counts under load — you may need a higher isolation level or a unique constraint
Throughput drops and you see lock wait timeouts — you may be at SERIALIZABLE when REPEATABLE READ would suffice

speakable_v2.cap: Know the four levels, their anomalies, and the defaults — then only increase isolation if you've confirmed an anomaly problem.

questions.question: What is transaction propagation in Spring and what is the difference between REQUIRED and REQUIRES_NEW?
questions.title: Spring Transaction Propagation: REQUIRED vs REQUIRES_NEW
questions.direct_answer: REQUIRED (default) joins an existing transaction if one exists, or starts a new one; REQUIRES_NEW always suspends the current transaction and starts a completely new one.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of transaction propagation — shows you know that @Transactional has behaviour beyond just 'wrap in a transaction'.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that REQUIRED is the default, or thinking every @Transactional always creates a new transaction.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a use case for REQUIRES_NEW: audit logging that should be committed even if the main transaction rolls back.

sections.title: How to Answer
Key Points
content: REQUIRED (default): join existing transaction or start new one — all in same unit
REQUIRES_NEW: suspend current transaction, start fresh, commit/rollback independently
Use REQUIRES_NEW when inner operation must commit regardless of outer rollback
Classic example: audit logging that must persist even if main transaction fails
Set with @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)

followup_questions: What happens to the outer transaction if REQUIRES_NEW inner transaction fails?

seo.metaTitle: Spring Transaction Propagation: REQUIRED vs REQUIRES_NEW
seo.metaDescription: Understand Spring transaction propagation — REQUIRED vs REQUIRES_NEW, when to use each, and an audit logging use case example.

speakable_v2.standard_example: normalized MySQL schema for a blog app with users, posts, and comments
speakable_v2.hook: Transaction propagation decides whether a nested method call joins your existing transaction or starts a fresh one.

groups.heading: REQUIRED (default)
groups.text: If there's already an active transaction, the method joins it. If there's none, a new one starts. All operations share the same unit — if the outer transaction rolls back, the inner one rolls back too.

groups.heading: REQUIRES_NEW
groups.text: Always suspends the current transaction and starts a completely new one. The inner method commits or rolls back independently. Even if the outer transaction later rolls back, the inner one's commit stands.

items: Use REQUIRED (default) when: the inner method is part of the same logical operation — publishing a post and updating the author's count
Use REQUIRES_NEW when: the inner operation must commit even if the outer fails — audit logging a failed post attempt

beats.text: In our blog: when a user publishes a post, we log the audit event. Use REQUIRES_NEW on logAuditEvent() — if the post publish fails and rolls back, the audit record still commits. That way you always have a record of the attempt.

speakable_v2.cap: REQUIRED is right for most cases; REQUIRES_NEW is the exception for operations that must commit regardless of the outer result.

questions.question: In practice, when do you actually need a database transaction?
questions.title: When Do You Need a Database Transaction?
questions.direct_answer: You need a transaction whenever two or more database operations must succeed or fail together — any multi-step operation where a partial update would leave data in an inconsistent state.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical judgment — knowing when to use transactions vs when a single operation doesn't need one.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Wrapping every single database call in @Transactional even when there's only one operation — unnecessary overhead.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name specific real-world scenarios: order creation, money transfer, inventory updates — and explain why each requires a transaction.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
Transactions are necessary when multiple operations must be treated as a single atomic unit.

Clear cases that need transactions:

Order creation: create an Order record, create OrderItem records, reduce inventory stock. If the stock reduction fails, you don't want an order with no stock adjustment. All three must succeed or all three must roll back.

Money transfer: deduct from one account, add to another. These two must happen together — no partial transfers.

User registration with profile: insert user record, insert profile record, insert default settings. A user without a profile in a system that requires one is invalid data.

Batch processing: if you're processing 100 records and fail on record 80, should 1-79 be committed? Maybe (separate transactions per record) or maybe not (all-or-nothing). Business requirement determines the transaction boundary.

When you don't need a transaction: a single read query, a single insert with no side effects, idempotent operations where partial completion is acceptable.

A practical guideline: if you can describe what 'partial success' means and it's a problem, you need a transaction. If partial success is fine or impossible, a transaction is overhead without benefit.

In Spring, put @Transactional on service methods that coordinate multiple repository calls — not on methods that make a single call.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Need transaction: when two or more operations must succeed or fail together
Examples: order creation, money transfer, user + profile insert
No transaction needed: single reads, single inserts with no side effects
Guideline: if partial success is a data integrity problem, use a transaction
Put @Transactional on service methods that coordinate multiple DB operations

followup_questions: Should @Transactional be on the service layer or the repository layer?

seo.metaTitle: When Do You Need a Database Transaction? Practical Guide
seo.metaDescription: Practical guidance on when to use database transactions in Spring Boot — real-world examples, @Transactional placement, and what doesn't need a transaction.

speakable_v2.standard_example: normalized MySQL schema for a blog app with users, posts, and comments
speakable_v2.hook: One rule for transactions: if partial success is a data integrity problem, you need a transaction.

beats.text: You're deciding which service methods need @Transactional. Wrapping everything is wasteful — transactions have overhead. Only operations where partial completion corrupts data need them.

items: Definitely need a transaction: publish post + update post_count (two writes that must succeed together)
Definitely need a transaction: user registration + default settings insert (partial creates broken accounts)
Don't need a transaction: single SELECT query, single INSERT with no side effects
Maybe need a transaction: depends on business rules — inserting a comment might or might not also update a count

beats.text: Put @Transactional on service methods that call multiple repository operations. Keep it off single-read methods. Spring Data JPA repositories are already transactional for individual calls — @Transactional on the service spans multiple calls into one unit.

items: You've put @Transactional on every single method including GET endpoints — you're holding DB connections unnecessarily
You're calling two repository saves without @Transactional — ask yourself what happens if the second one fails

speakable_v2.cap: Ask: what does partial success look like? If it's a data integrity problem — use a transaction. If not — skip it.
